project_name: Number Portability Administration Center Service Management System
initial_requirements: Telecommunications service providers need a shared administration system for moving customers' telephone numbers between provider networks. The system should receive information from the old and new providers, validate and coordinate their requests, activate agreed routing changes, and distribute updated portability data to participating networks. Operations personnel also need transaction history, conflict handling, reporting, and audit capabilities to keep provider records synchronized.

slots.key: Transaction volumes and geographic coverage
slots.value: Nationwide coverage across all participating regions; volume can spike during business hours, end-of-month cycles, and campaign periods when providers push many migrations at once, so the system must handle bursts without delaying validation or routing updates.

slots.key: Operational timing and cutover windows by carrier
slots.value: Carriers can have different daily processing windows for accepting submissions, reviewing pending requests, and allowing activation. Some carriers only process ports during business hours, while others support scheduled cutovers in specific time slots. The shared system must respect those windows and not force activation outside them. It also needs to accommodate cutoff times for same-day versus next-day processing, because that determines when a request can move from validation to approval and routing activation.

topics.topic_content: Business vocabulary used in portability operations

slots.key: Reference definitions for porting request, routing change, and portability record
slots.value: A porting request is the formal transaction opened to move one or more numbers from the old provider to the new provider for a specific customer. A routing change is the operational update that tells the networks where to send traffic for those numbers after the port is approved. A portability record is the authoritative data entry kept for each number or transaction so all participants can see its current status, ownership history, and routing state; it is used to keep everyone synchronized and to support audit and reporting later.

topics.topic_content: Exception-driven business events during port coordination

slots.key: Rework events caused by mismatched provider submissions
slots.value: Conflict handling; flag the request as discrepant or awaiting correction, keep it out of the normal approval flow until the mismatch is resolved, record the mismatch details, who identified it, and any revised submission or confirmation from the providers; once corrected, move back into normal process state while retaining discrepancy history; if unresolved, close as failed or canceled with a clear reason code. Exception and conflict handling are the next highest priority, and conflict resolution should include clear status tracking so the process can keep moving. The dispute should only be resolved by designated operations staff with authority over number portability, and for certain cases by an approved escalation owner if the providers can’t agree. If the conflict affects the correctness of routing or the ownership of the number, work should pause until it’s resolved; if it’s only a documentation mismatch and the live routing is still safe, a provisional decision can let the process continue.

slots.key: Duplicate portability request blocking and matching rule
slots.value: Block true duplicates rather than letting them proceed. If a new submission matches an existing open request, warn the operator and prevent it from going further until the prior case is resolved or explicitly closed. Treat it as a duplicate when the same telephone number is already in an open or pending portability case; possibly also when customer/account reference and service address match closely enough to indicate the same port, with the exact threshold to be defined carefully with operations. If the existing request is still active in the same number, reject the new one rather than queue it, because different stages still mean there is only one live port path for that number. The system can link the attempted submission to the existing case as a related event, but it should not create a second independent workflow. If the earlier request is in a terminal state like closed, canceled, or failed, then a new request can be accepted normally. Default handling should be one active request per number at any time, with exact stage-by-stage handling to be made explicit in the rules. The console should also reject duplicate submissions or those in conflict with an existing pending or completed transaction.

slots.key: Rejection and correction validation error categories
slots.value: Missing fields, formatting issues, and some data-entry mistakes are correctable by operations staff and can be resubmitted after fixing. Existing transaction conflicts, duplicate in-progress requests, and scheduling overlaps should be held or blocked until the conflict is cleared. Authorization problems, eligibility disputes, and underlying provider data mismatches should be escalated to the responsible team. Incoming portability updates with the same timestamp or out-of-order sequence may be held for review if they still look valid, rather than immediately applied.

slots.value: Authorization problems, eligibility disputes, and underlying provider data mismatches should be escalated to the responsible team because console staff usually shouldn’t override them on their own; if there’s no approved alternate channel, an authorized operations lead or the responsible integration team must confirm the channel is fixed or an approved fallback is in place before release resumes. If an incoming update conflicts with the active state in a way that suggests a duplicate, replay, or bad provider feed, it should be rejected or sent back for reprocessing rather than applied automatically. For anything that touches regulatory obligations or industry-defined rules, escalation is required before routing proceeds, especially if there’s any risk of violating porting rules or misrouting a live number.

slots.key: Exception queue item inclusion and prioritization
slots.value: The exception queue should exclude pure informational updates, already-closed transactions, duplicate notifications, and system health or interface outages, which should instead be handled in an operations incident view rather than the port coordination queue. Items blocked by data validation failures should be tagged differently from those blocked by compliance approval issues so staff can distinguish business exceptions from technical exceptions. The queue should still show only blocked items, items needing manual approval, and items with an active exception, excluding ordinary completed transactions. Overdue items should automatically escalate after a defined threshold; items near cutover should be pushed to the top even if they arrived later; items delayed on the organization’s side should be treated as more urgent than items waiting on an external provider; and authorized supervisors may manually reorder items for customer-impact reasons, with the priority change logged for auditability.

slots.key: Transaction history and auditability priority
slots.value: Transaction history and auditability are essential for control and traceability, but they are secondary to live operational functions in priority. When needed during an active issue, the history should be available immediately for diagnosis and coordination of a live port, for a provider dispute, a suspected fraud or unauthorized port, an unresolved timeout that is blocking the transaction, or when a manual override or reversal is being considered so staff can review the full trail before acting; for post-incident review or routine audit, it can be available after the live operation is resolved, provided it is complete and searchable. If it’s just a normal completed transaction with no active issue, immediate access is less critical.

slots.value: Reject a request if it is a duplicate or if it conflicts with an existing pending, completed, or scheduled porting transaction or cutover; it must not enter active processing. revisions.new_value: Block true duplicates rather than let them proceed. If a new submission matches an existing open request, warn the operator and prevent it from going further until the prior case is resolved or explicitly closed. Treat it as a duplicate when the same telephone number is already in an open or pending portability case, and possibly also when the customer/account reference and service address match closely enough to indicate the same port; the exact threshold should be defined carefully with operations.

slots.key: Exception and disruption event handling during port coordination
slots.value: Capture failed validation, carrier rejection, missed cutoff, conflicting requests, activation failure, cancellation, rollback, and manual intervention; each event creates a traceable status change and an exception record. Depending on the event, the request pauses for correction, routes to manual review, or moves to a terminal failed or canceled state. Preserve the original request data and resolution notes for later reconciliation and reporting. When a port request is reworked because the old and new provider submissions do not match, the system should flag the request as discrepant or awaiting correction, keep it out of the normal approval flow until the mismatch is resolved, record the mismatch details, who identified it, and any revised submission or confirmation from the providers, retain the discrepancy history after correction, and close it as failed or canceled with a clear reason code if unresolved.

slots.key: Administration console tasks for portability operations
slots.value: Review incoming provider requests, check validation results, resolve exceptions or conflicts, approve or correct records where authorized, reject invalid submissions with a clear reason and correction guidance, and keep minor issues in draft or correction state until they pass validation. The console should distinguish missing required fields, format or data-quality errors, authorization problems, ineligible numbers, duplicate requests, and conflicts with an existing porting transaction or scheduled cutover so staff can tell whether they can fix the issue themselves or whether it needs referral or escalation. Also monitor routing updates and network distributions, search transaction history, generate reports, and review audit trails. Missing fields, formatting issues, and some data-entry mistakes are correctable by operations staff and can be resubmitted once fixed. Existing transaction conflicts, duplicate in progress cases, and scheduling overlaps should be held or blocked until the conflict is cleared. Authorization problems, eligibility disputes, and underlying provider data mismatches should be escalated to the responsible team.

topics.topic_content: Coordination, approval, and routing change activation

slots.key: Agreement confirmation between providers
slots.value: Coordinate provider requests and activate agreed routing changes; newer updates should be accepted as the latest state only when they have a clearly newer sequence or timestamp and match the expected transaction context. If timestamps are the same or the sequence is out of order but the content still looks valid, hold it for review so an operator can compare it with the current record before anything is overwritten. If it conflicts with the active state in a way that suggests a duplicate, replay, or bad feed from a provider, reject it or send it back for reprocessing rather than applying it automatically. The current state should be shown only after the update has passed those checks and been confirmed as the latest valid one.

Error messages should point to the exact field or condition, state what was expected versus what was found, and, where possible, give the next action in plain language so the user can fix the issue without interpreting a technical error code. Missing fields, formatting issues, and some data-entry mistakes are correctable by operations staff and can be resubmitted once fixed. Requests with an existing transaction conflict, a duplicate in progress, or a scheduling overlap should be held or blocked until the conflict is cleared. Authorization problems, eligibility disputes, or mismatches in underlying provider data should be escalated to the responsible team.

slots.key: Routing activation timing and cutover rules
slots.value: Support carrier-specific cutoff rules for accepting new submissions, with some providers rolling submissions after the cutoff to the next business day. For pending reviews and approvals, the system must respect whether the carrier processes them continuously or only within a defined business window, because that affects when a port can move forward. For activation, the cutover trigger has to follow the carrier’s allowed activation window and any same-day versus next-day rule tied to the request timestamp and approval time. The shared system should also reflect holiday or exceptional maintenance window changes without requiring manual overrides for every transaction.

slots.key: Migration validation and reconciliation
slots.value: Migrated records should be validated against the source before cutover, with exceptions logged. Records that cannot be mapped cleanly should go to a dedicated data-mapping exception queue for manual review by operations staff with provider-domain knowledge, and possibly a supervisor if the mismatch affects a large batch or a critical customer. Items stay out of cutover only when the mapping issue could create a wrong routing or an incomplete portability record; minor nonessential field mismatches would usually proceed and be flagged for cleanup. If an item is still unresolved at cutover, it should be kept blocked and escalated immediately rather than forced through, with a formal hold and audit note. The deciding rule for release at cutover is whether releasing the record would risk incorrect number routing, loss of service, or a breach of regulatory or provider agreement obligations. If any of those risks are present, the record should stay blocked and be escalated to a designated operations lead or duty manager for an explicit decision. It can be released only with a documented exception if the business owner accepts the risk, the impact is limited, and there is a clear rollback or correction path after cutover. The exception must record the reason, approver, and expiry or follow-up action so it does not become an unmanaged permanent state. The dispute should only be resolved by designated operations staff with authority over number portability, and for certain cases by an approved escalation owner if the providers can’t agree. If the conflict affects the correctness of routing or the ownership of the number, work should pause until it’s resolved; if it’s only a documentation mismatch and the live routing is still safe, a provisional decision can let the process continue. For anything that touches regulatory obligations or industry-defined rules, escalation is required before routing proceeds, especially if there’s any risk of violating porting rules or misrouting a live number.

slots.key: Cutover and retention of old records
slots.value: The legacy records should be retained for as long as business, regulatory, and audit requirements call for, with the retention period defined by policy rather than left open-ended. The retention window should be a fixed policy window, and once that window ends the records can be disposed of unless there is a reason to hold them longer. Any active dispute, audit, litigation, regulatory inquiry, fraud investigation, or legal hold should pause disposal until it is formally cleared. If a case is still open or could reasonably become evidence, the record should be retained beyond the normal schedule. Access should be tightly restricted to authorized operations, compliance, audit, and support staff, with normal users kept in the new system only. Staff should consult the old record for historical disputes, unresolved transactions that originated before cutover, regulatory inquiries, and reconciliation issues between the old and new systems; for routine post-cutover ports with a clean history in the new system, rely on the new record alone.

revisions.new_value: After cutover, the new system becomes the system of record, while old records are retained for reference and dispute handling.

slots.key: Portability record lifecycle and audit trail control
slots.value: A record should become effectively immutable once a portability record has been approved, especially after routing has been activated, except for tightly controlled correction fields or an authorized amendment process. Only designated operations users with strong audit tracking should be able to make post-approval changes, and the system should retain the prior version rather than overwrite it. If a correction happens later, the system must keep the full change history, the reason for the amendment, who approved it, and any source evidence or provider confirmation tied to that correction, so the original decision and subsequent changes can always be proven. Corrections to approved records should be authorized only by a limited set of privileged users, usually supervisors or designated operations leads, not general staff, and they should include an attached reason and supporting evidence such as a provider notice, audit reference, or ticket number. The original approved record should remain intact, with the correction saved as a new version or amendment entry rather than overwritten in place.

slots.key: Duplicate portability request handling
slots.value: Block true duplicates rather than allow them through; if a new submission matches an existing open request, warn the operator and prevent it from proceeding until the prior case is resolved or explicitly closed. If the existing request is still active in the same number, reject the new one rather than queue it; the attempted submission may be linked to the existing case as a related event, but it must not create a second independent workflow. If the earlier request is in a terminal state like closed, canceled, or failed, a new request can be accepted normally.

slots.key: Expedited change trigger conditions
slots.value: Expedited changes should be triggered when the issue is already causing failed port activations, incorrect routing, or a material backlog blocking customer moves. They also qualify when the defect affects multiple providers, has a compliance or service-level deadline within the current cycle, or is getting worse fast. They should not be used if the issue is contained, has a safe workaround, and the next release is close enough that delaying the fix keeps business impact manageable. If the problem is stopping or corrupting live portability operations right now, or is causing failed ports, wrong routing, or a compliance exposure that cannot be contained, it should be handled as an immediate fix; if the impact is annoying but contained and a workaround preserves correct operation, defer it to the next release. sections.section_content: Portability Data, Transaction Records, and External Interfaces

topics.topic_content: Core portability data model and record lifecycle

slots.key: Portability record contents
slots.value: A portability record is the authoritative data entry kept for each number or transaction so all participants can see its current status, ownership history, and routing state; it is used to keep everyone synchronized and to support audit and reporting later. During migration, old data must be mapped carefully into the new system so transaction history and current routing status are preserved. It must also preserve the original request data and any resolution notes so the disruption can be reconciled later and reported on. Staff should see the transaction identifiers, the provider names involved, the timestamps, the current status, the decision trail, and any validation or exception notes tied to the case. They also need enough subscriber reference data to match the case correctly, but not necessarily the full customer profile. For highly sensitive data exports, the record/logging should also capture what subset was exported, the exact purpose, whether it was encrypted or masked, any later transformation such as splitting, merging, or reformatting, and who handled each step; if the export is split into multiple files, the original export event must remain tied to all derived files to preserve chain of custody.

slots.key: Record status progression and retention
slots.value: A portability record is created as soon as the submission is accepted into the system, then updated as it moves through validation, approval, and activation with a clear status trail. Once the request is approved and especially once routing activation is scheduled or executed, the record becomes tightly controlled so only authorized changes or cancellation actions can happen. If there is a rollback, rejection, cancellation, or other disruption, the system does not erase the original record; it marks it superseded or closed with the final outcome and keeps the history intact for a full audit trail of what happened, when it happened, and why. Exceptions create traceable status changes and exception records, and the request may pause for correction, route to manual review, or move into a terminal failed or canceled state. In the event of a provider mismatch, the request should be flagged as discrepant or awaiting correction and kept out of the normal approval flow until resolved; if corrected, it returns to the normal process state while retaining the discrepancy history, and if unresolved it is closed as failed or canceled with a clear reason code. If a new submission matches an existing open request, the system should warn the operator and prevent it from going further until the prior case is resolved or explicitly closed. For migration, at minimum every migrated record must be validated against the source, any exceptions must be logged, and the original import evidence must be retained for audit so it is clear what was accepted, what was rejected, and why. Migration mapping exceptions go to a dedicated data-mapping exception queue for manual review by operations staff with provider-domain knowledge, and possibly a supervisor if the mismatch affects a large batch or a critical customer. Records stay out of cutover only when the mapping issue could create a wrong routing or an incomplete portability record; minor nonessential field mismatches usually proceed and are flagged for cleanup. If cutover arrives and an item is still unresolved, it is kept blocked and escalated immediately with a formal hold and audit note, and only the affected record is delayed rather than the whole migration if just one item is unresolved. When a mapping issue is still unresolved at cutover, the release decision should be based on whether releasing it would risk incorrect number routing, loss of service, or a breach of regulatory or provider agreement obligations; if any of those risks are present, it should stay blocked and be escalated to a designated operations lead or duty manager for an explicit decision. It can only be released with a documented exception if the business owner accepts the risk, the impact is limited, and there is a clear rollback or correction path after cutover, and the exception must record the reason, approver, and expiry or follow-up action so it does not become an unmanaged permanent state. If a record is still under reconciliation or has an open exception, it should be held back from general distribution until the discrepancy is resolved or a formal exception is approved. For clean records, distribution should happen as part of the normal publish cycle so everyone gets the same version at roughly the same time. If one provider is out of sync, the specific record should be paused rather than pushing inconsistent data into the network.

In the event of a provider mismatch, the request should be flagged as discrepant or awaiting correction and kept out of the normal approval flow until resolved; if corrected, it returns to the normal process state while retaining the discrepancy history, and if unresolved it is closed as failed or canceled with a clear reason code. If a new submission matches an existing open request, the system should warn the operator and prevent it from going further until the prior case is resolved or explicitly closed. For migration, at minimum every migrated record must be validated against the source, any exceptions must be logged, and the original import evidence must be retained for audit so it is clear what was accepted, what was rejected, and why. Migration mapping exceptions go to a dedicated data-mapping exception queue for manual review by operations staff with provider-domain knowledge, and possibly a supervisor if the mismatch affects a large batch or a critical customer. Records stay out of cutover only when the mapping issue could create a wrong routing or an incomplete portability record; minor nonessential field mismatches usually proceed and are flagged for cleanup. If cutover arrives and an item is still unresolved, it is kept blocked and escalated immediately with a formal hold and audit note, and only the affected record is delayed rather than the whole migration if just one item is unresolved. When a mapping issue is still unresolved at cutover, the release decision should be based on whether releasing it would risk incorrect number routing, loss of service, or a breach of regulatory or provider agreement obligations; if any of those risks are present, it should stay blocked and be escalated to a designated operations lead or duty manager for an explicit decision. It can only be released with a documented exception if the business owner accepts the risk, the impact is limited, and there is a clear rollback or correction path after cutover, and the exception must record the reason, approver, and expiry or follow-up action so it does not become an unmanaged permanent state. If a record is still under reconciliation or has an open exception, it should be held back from general distribution until the discrepancy is resolved or a formal exception is approved. For clean records, distribution should happen as part of the normal publish cycle so everyone gets the same version at roughly the same time. If one provider is out of sync, the specific record should be paused rather than pushing inconsistent data into the network.

slots.key: Regulatory compliance handling requirements
slots.value: Support applicable telecommunications portability regulations in the jurisdiction, including timely processing, accurate routing, evidence of who approved what and when, tamper-evident transaction and audit records for disputes or regulator reviews, access controls, traceability, and compliance reporting support; once a portability record has been approved and especially after routing has been activated, it should become effectively immutable except for tightly controlled correction fields or an authorized amendment process, with only designated operations users able to change anything after that point under strong audit tracking, and the system should retain the prior version rather than overwrite it. If a correction happens later, the system must keep the full change history, the reason for the amendment, who approved it, and any source evidence or provider confirmation tied to that correction so the original decision and subsequent changes can always be proven. Corrections to approved records should be authorized only by a limited set of privileged users, usually supervisors or designated operations leads, not general staff; they should include an attached reason and supporting evidence such as a provider notice, audit reference, or ticket number; and the original approved record should remain intact with the correction saved as a new version or amendment entry rather than overwritten in place. Sensitive data should be protected through role-based access, with sensitive subscriber details masked or redacted unless a higher clearance or a specific investigation justifies full visibility.

slots.key: Legal retention and regulator format details
slots.value: Exact retention periods are defined by policy to satisfy business, regulatory, and audit requirements rather than left open-ended; legacy records are retained for as long as those requirements call for. In practice, the retention should be a fixed policy window. Once that window ends, the records can be disposed of unless there is a reason to hold them longer. Active disputes, audits, litigation, regulatory inquiries, fraud investigations, or legal holds should pause disposal until formally cleared. If a case is still open or could reasonably become evidence, the record should be retained beyond the normal schedule. Access to legacy records is tightly restricted to authorized operations, compliance, audit, and support staff, with normal users kept in the new system only. When a matter is formally opened or a written notice identifying the case as subject to hold is received, whichever comes first, that event should mark the start of the hold, and the opening notice or case ID should be stored against the affected records. Responsibility for placing the hold should sit with compliance, legal, audit, or fraud management depending on the matter type, and the same function should formally close the hold; operations may flag the issue but are not the final authority to start or lift it. Operations should be able to see hold status history, including the date and time it was placed or lifted, the person or role that authorized it, the stated reason or reference number tied to the case, and any related notes such as dispute ID, investigation number, or legal notice. Reporting should show the full sequence of hold actions, any changes to the affected record set, and whether the hold was active during any disposal or retention decision so staff can tell exactly who did what and whether it was properly authorized. If only part of the file needs to stay protected, the hold should apply just to the relevant records or fields when they can be safely segregated; the protected portion should remain unchanged until the hold is lifted, while the non-sensitive parts follow normal retention and disposal rules. If the file cannot be reliably split, the safer rule is to keep the whole record set under hold. Sensitive material should remain access-controlled and redacted in ordinary views during the extended retention period. The exact triggers for extending a disposal pause are left undecided for now and should be defined later in the records policy rather than hard-coded into system behavior.

slots.key: Duplicate portability request handling and matching rule
slots.value: Block true duplicates rather than let them proceed. If an existing request is still active for the same number, reject the new request rather than queueing it; the new attempt may be linked to the existing case as a related event, but it must not create a second independent workflow. If the earlier request is in a terminal state such as closed, canceled, or failed, a new request can be accepted normally. The default rule should be one active request per number at any time.

revisions.new_value: Block true duplicates rather than let them proceed. For duplicate detection, treat a request as duplicate when the same telephone number is already in an open or pending portability case; possibly also when the customer/account reference and service address match closely enough to indicate the same port. The exact business threshold should be defined carefully with operations.

slots.key: Release hold and manual clearance for noncompliant interface
slots.value: If no approved alternate channel is available, the console must block the release and keep the transaction in a held state rather than forcing it through. Release can move forward only after the noncompliant interface is brought back into approved status or an approved alternate channel is set up and confirmed by the responsible team, with documented approval from operations and the integration or network side before the hold is cleared. An exception path may be allowed if policy permits a temporary fallback for urgent service continuity, but it must be tightly controlled, logged, and time-limited; if there is no approved fallback, the transaction stays held until the normal compliant path is restored.

slots.key: Portability state update validation and out-of-sequence handling
slots.value: Portability state updates should be accepted as the latest state when the incoming update has a clearly newer sequence or timestamp and matches the expected transaction context. If timestamps are the same or the sequence is out of order but the content still looks valid, it should be held for review so an operator can compare it with the current record before anything is overwritten. If it conflicts with the active state in a way that suggests a duplicate, replay, or bad provider feed, it should be rejected or sent back for reprocessing rather than applied automatically.

revisions.new_value: Portability state updates must not be treated as current immediately on arrival. The console should compare timestamps, transaction sequence, and source authority so that older or out-of-order changes do not overwrite a newer confirmed state. If a record falls outside the allowed tolerance or arrives in the wrong sequence, it should be held for review or reprocessing rather than marked current. The current state should be shown only after the update has passed those checks and been confirmed as the latest valid one.

slots.value: A technical incident usually shows up as a system, interface, or connectivity problem affecting multiple transactions, while a business exception is tied to one specific port request or approval path. The practical sign is whether the action needed is to fix the transaction itself or to restore the underlying service.

slots.key: Synchronization issue open-vs-workaround decision rule
slots.value: Keep a synchronization issue open for provider action when the fix requires the originating provider to correct source data or confirm a disputed status. Use a temporary workaround or manual reconciliation only when the issue is limited, reversible, and can be handled with an audit trail without changing the underlying business truth. The choice should come down to impact, urgency, and reversibility: if the mismatch is affecting live routing, a publish deadline, or a large set of records, and we can safely isolate the workaround to one item with a clear rollback, then it can be justified; if it’s just a reporting delay or low-priority discrepancy, we should leave it open for the originating provider to correct. A workaround is acceptable without provider confirmation only when the operational risk of waiting is higher than the risk of temporarily handling it ourselves, and it must be clearly marked as provisional, time-limited, and reviewed so it does not become accepted as the normal state.

topics.topic_content: Distribution of updated portability data to participating networks

slots.key: Distribution recipients and synchronization frequency
slots.value: Participating networks, including the central administration or portability operator role and, in some cases, network or carrier participants that consume the updated routing data; they need access to view transaction status, receive notifications, and use the updated portability information so their routing stays aligned. Updated portability data should go first to the networks directly affected by the change and needed for routing accuracy, especially the donor and recipient providers. For clean records, distribution should happen as part of the normal publish cycle so everyone gets the same version at roughly the same time. If the record is complete, approved, and within the cutover window, it should go out in the next normal publish cycle without waiting for extra manual review. Delay only if there is a pending validation run, a dependency on another record in the same batch, or the distribution window has already closed for that cycle.

slots.value: Per-network configuration is supported; each network uses its agreed interface, provided it meets required security and delivery standards.

revisions.new_value: Per-network configuration is supported; each network uses its agreed interface, provided it meets required security and delivery standards.

slots.key: Acknowledgement and retransmission behavior
slots.value: If a provider message fails to arrive, is malformed, or cannot be processed, the default rule is to hold the affected update and retry delivery or processing on a configured schedule rather than proceeding partially. If it still fails after the retry window, it moves into an exception state and operations are alerted so they can investigate and, if needed, use a manual or alternate path. Staff should be alerted immediately for anything that blocks a cutover or leaves routing data inconsistent, and otherwise after repeated failures or if the message is malformed in a way that cannot be auto-corrected. If there is a discrepancy, the operations team manages the exception and chases the originating provider rather than silently fixing it without trace. If a record is still under reconciliation or has an open exception, it should be held back from general distribution until the discrepancy is resolved or a formal exception is approved. If one provider is out of sync, pause that specific record rather than pushing inconsistent data into the network.

topics.topic_content: Eligibility and decision rules for number porting

slots.key: Porting eligibility criteria
slots.value: Cross-provider porting is needed when a customer moves service from one telecommunications provider to another and wants to keep the same phone number; it also applies when consolidating services, changing from mobile to fixed or vice versa, or moving a number between brands or network partners still within the portability environment.

revisions.new_value: Cross-provider porting is needed when a customer moves service from one telecommunications provider to another and wants to keep the same phone number; it also applies when consolidating services, changing from mobile to fixed or vice versa, or moving a number between brands or network partners still within the portability environment.

slots.key: Provider approval conditions
slots.value: The old provider accepts the port request before the port can proceed; approval is the point at which the old provider has accepted the request.

revisions.new_value: The old provider reviews the port request and either accepts or rejects it based on the customer data and any outstanding issues; the old provider checks eligibility, identifies conflicts or discrepancies, and releases the number once the port is approved.

slots.key: Time windows and cutoff rules
slots.value: Routing activation or cutover is the actual switch where traffic is updated so the number points to the new provider's network, and it must happen only after the request is fully approved and within the allowed timing window. The system should store carrier-specific cutoff rules for each stage: some providers accept new submissions only until a certain time and roll later submissions to the next business day; pending reviews and approvals may be processed continuously or only within a defined business window; activation must follow the carrier’s allowed activation window and any same-day versus next-day rule tied to request timestamp and approval time; and the system should reflect holiday or exceptional-maintenance window changes without manual overrides.

slots.key: Request validation and rejection handling
slots.value: Before acceptance, the console must distinguish between missing required fields, format or data-quality errors, authorization problems, ineligible numbers, duplicate requests, and conflicts with an existing porting transaction or scheduled cutover. Missing fields, formatting issues, and some data-entry mistakes are correctable by operations staff and can be fixed then resubmitted. Requests with an existing transaction conflict, a duplicate in progress, or a scheduling overlap should be held or blocked until the conflict is cleared. Authorization problems, eligibility disputes, and cases where the underlying provider data does not match should be escalated to the responsible team, since console staff should not override those themselves.

If validation fails or required information is missing, the console must reject the submission with a clear reason and tell the user what needs to be corrected; minor issues that can be edited may remain in a draft or correction state, but must not enter active processing until validation passes.

topics.topic_content: Legal, regulatory, and industry obligations for portability operations

slots.key: Regulatory compliance obligations
slots.value: Support applicable telecommunications portability regulations in the jurisdiction, especially timely processing, accurate routing, evidence of who approved what and when, preservation of transaction and audit records for the required retention period, tamper-evident records for dispute or regulator review, access controls, traceability, and compliance reporting support; once a portability record has been approved and especially after routing has been activated, it should become effectively immutable except for tightly controlled correction fields or an authorized amendment process, with only designated operations users able to change anything after that point under strong audit tracking; corrections to approved records should be authorized only by a limited set of privileged users such as supervisors or designated operations leads, not general staff, and must include an attached reason plus supporting evidence such as a provider notice, audit reference, or ticket number, with the original approved record preserved and the correction recorded as a new version or amendment entry rather than overwritten in place; if an unresolved mapping issue at cutover would risk incorrect number routing, loss of service, or a breach of regulatory or provider agreement obligations, the record should stay blocked and be escalated to a designated operations lead or duty manager for an explicit decision, and it can be released only with a documented exception accepted by the business owner when the impact is limited and there is a clear rollback or correction path after cutover; controlled changes should follow a regular release cadence, with only well-tested, approved changes going into the shared portability process, and an expedited path is allowed only for urgent operational risk with documented impact assessment and explicit approval from the right operations authority; expedited change should be triggered only by conditions actively hurting service, such as a routing defect, a widespread sync failure, a compliance deadline, or a live porting incident that can't wait for the next cycle, and should not be used for convenience or routine backlog clearing. Before bypassing the normal release cycle, require a documented impact assessment, a clear rollback or fallback plan, approval from operations and the program's change control owner, and documented urgency reason plus expected business impact for later audit. For anything that touches regulatory obligations or industry-defined rules, escalation is required before routing proceeds, especially if there is any risk of violating porting rules or misrouting a live number; the escalation path should be explicit and logged, and when a regulatory or industry-rule conflict arises it should go to the designated portability compliance contact or the industry authority that governs numbering rules, depending on the operating model. The process should pause if the conflict could lead to an illegal port, wrong routing, or customer harm; it may continue provisionally only when the risk is low, the routing outcome is still reversible, and there is documented approval to proceed while escalation is pending. Provisional continuation should only be allowed when the port is operationally safe to proceed, meaning we’re not likely to misroute traffic or violate a hard regulatory rule. That usually fits cases where the issue is clerical, missing confirmation, or an interpretation question that can be corrected without changing the live routing outcome. Before that can happen, explicit approval from the designated compliance or operations authority is required, along with a documented reason for proceeding, the risks accepted, and the exact limits of the provisional action. It should also be time-bound and recorded in the transaction history so it can be reviewed or rolled back if needed. At cutover, legacy records should be retained for as long as business, regulatory, and audit requirements call for, with the retention period defined by policy rather than left open-ended; the exact retention period is not yet known and depends on the regulator, telecom rules, and internal records policy, but it should be a fixed policy window, after which records may be disposed of unless a reason exists to hold them longer. Access should be tightly restricted to authorized operations, compliance, audit, and support staff, with normal users kept in the new system only. During migration, legacy records should be read-only for most staff; view access should be limited to authorized operations, migration, and audit personnel; copying or exporting should be restricted to approved migration tasks and logged; editing should generally be blocked unless there is a controlled correction process with explicit approval. Exceptions should be limited to a small set of unusually authorized cases such as a data fix or investigation, and even then access should be time-bound and recorded. Normal users and other teams should not get broad access just because the records are legacy. For highly sensitive provider or subscriber data in approved migration exports, logs should capture more detail: what subset was exported, the exact purpose, whether it was encrypted or masked, any transformation step such as splitting, merging, or reformatting, and who handled each step. If the export was later split into multiple files, the original export event should remain tied to all derived files to preserve chain of custody. For normal sensitivity data, the logging can be lighter, but for high-risk records this level of detail is mandatory.

corrections to approved records should be authorized only by a limited set of privileged users such as supervisors or designated operations leads, not general staff, and must include an attached reason plus supporting evidence such as a provider notice, audit reference, or ticket number, with the original approved record preserved and the correction recorded as a new version or amendment entry rather than overwritten in place; if an unresolved mapping issue at cutover would risk incorrect number routing, loss of service, or a breach of regulatory or provider agreement obligations, the record should stay blocked and be escalated to a designated operations lead or duty manager for an explicit decision, and it can be released only with a documented exception accepted by the business owner when the impact is limited and there is a clear rollback or correction path after cutover; controlled changes should follow a regular release cadence, with only well-tested, approved changes going into the shared portability process, and an expedited path is allowed only for urgent operational risk with documented impact assessment and explicit approval from the right operations authority; expedited change should be triggered only by conditions actively hurting service, such as a routing defect, a widespread sync failure, a compliance deadline, or a live porting incident that can't wait for the next cycle, and should not be used for convenience or routine backlog clearing. Before bypassing the normal release cycle, require a documented impact assessment, a clear rollback or fallback plan, approval from operations and the program's change control owner, and documented urgency reason plus expected business impact for later audit.

slots.value: The regulator usually expects standardized content like request counts, completion times, failures, dispute cases, and status breakdowns, often in a specific template or file type they prescribe; the system should generate the exact required structure, and it should also support alternative presentations for ad hoc audits, internal management reporting, or one-off regulator extractions. slots.key: Documented exception governance for unresolved cutover issues
slots.value: A workaround or manual handling is justified when the mismatch affects live routing, a publish deadline, or a large set of records, provided it can be safely isolated to one item with a clear rollback; if it’s just a reporting delay or low-priority discrepancy, the issue should stay open for the originating provider to correct. A workaround without provider confirmation is acceptable only when the operational risk of waiting is higher than the risk of temporarily handling it ourselves, and it must be clearly marked as provisional, time-limited, and reviewed so it does not become accepted as the normal state.

revisions.new_value: A documented exception is allowed only when the business owner accepts the risk, the impact is limited, and there is a clear rollback or correction path after cutover; the exception must record the reason, approver, and expiry or follow-up action so it does not become an unmanaged permanent state

revisions.new_value: A documented exception is allowed only when the issue is low impact, tightly bounded to a specific record or small batch, and there is no material risk of wrong routing or service disruption if proceeding; it also needs a clear compensating control, such as a planned correction window, so it is not left open-ended. If the business owner is unavailable or declines to accept the risk, approval should fall to a delegated operations manager or duty executive with the same authority level; if no one at that level is reachable, the item remains blocked, and frontline staff should not make the call on their own.

slots.value: The history must be available immediately when the issue is active and operations staff are diagnosing or coordinating a live port, or when there is a regulatory or customer-impact investigation underway; additionally, immediate access is needed for provider disputes, suspected fraud or unauthorized ports, unresolved timeouts that are blocking the transaction, and any case where a manual override or reversal is being considered. At cutover, staff should consult the old record for historical disputes, unresolved transactions that originated before cutover, regulatory inquiries, and reconciliation issues between the old and new systems; routine post-cutover ports with a clean history in the new system should rely on the new record alone.

slots.key: Privacy masking and role-based access for porting case data
slots.value: Personal subscriber details such as full contact information, account content, and any other data not needed to resolve the port should be limited, masked, or redacted; access should be role-based so operations staff see what they need, while fuller visibility is reserved for higher clearance or a specific investigation. Unmasking should only happen when the restricted data is genuinely necessary to resolve an active porting issue, such as a suspected fraud case, identity mismatch, dispute over ownership, or a regulatory review that can't be completed with the limited view. It should not be opened just for convenience or general curiosity. Before broader access is granted, approval is required from a designated supervisor, compliance lead, or security-controlled role, the reason must be recorded in the case history, and the access itself must be logged, including who approved it, who viewed it, and for how long the elevated access was used. If the sensitive part can be cleanly separated without changing the meaning or evidentiary value of the rest, then the sensitive portion can be held and redacted while the non-sensitive portion follows normal retention; if separating it would break the record’s context, make the record incomplete, or create a risk of accidental disclosure, then the whole file should stay under hold. The practical rule is whether integrity and traceability can be preserved while limiting access to only what needs protection.

sections.section_content: Operator Experience, Response Behavior, and Accuracy

topics.topic_content: Administration console usability for operations personnel

slots.key: Operator workflow efficiency needs
slots.value: Operations personnel need administration capabilities for reviewing incoming provider requests, checking validation results, resolving exceptions or conflicts, approving or correcting records where authorized, monitoring the status of routing updates and network distributions, searching transaction history, generating reports, and reviewing audit trails. Effectiveness depends on a clear status view, fast search, and obvious exception handling with minimal steps for common actions; it becomes difficult if the console is cluttered, requires jumping between screens for routine work, or does not clearly separate alerts and approvals from informational items. They also need a very clear status dashboard that separates requests into ready for approval, pending correction, pending escalation, and already activated, with each state shown consistently across the console, and activated routing changes must be unmistakable so they no longer look like items waiting for processing. Exception records should be visually distinct with a clear banner or status label such as temporary approval that stays visible until the exception is closed. Pure informational updates, already-closed transactions, and duplicate notifications should be excluded from the normal exception queue and handled separately; system health or interface outages should be kept in an operations incident view rather than the port coordination queue. Data validation failures and compliance approval issues should be tagged differently so staff can distinguish business exceptions from technical ones.

slots.key: Invalid or incomplete request handling
slots.value: If validation fails or required information is missing, the console should distinguish the reason for rejection or hold, point to the exact field or condition, say what was expected versus what was found, and give the next action in plain language so the user can fix it without interpreting a technical error code. Minor issues may remain in a draft or correction state, but must not enter active processing until validation passes. Missing fields, formatting issues, and some data-entry mistakes should be correctable by operations staff and then resubmitted once fixed. Requests with an existing transaction conflict, a duplicate in progress, or a scheduling overlap should be held or blocked until the conflict is cleared, because those affect coordination rather than simple input quality. Authorization problems, eligibility disputes, or cases where the underlying provider data does not match should be escalated to the responsible team, since staff in the console usually shouldn’t override those on their own. For exception handling, the console should make warnings and blockers obvious, with a short reason and the next required action right next to the record.

topics.topic_content: System responsiveness and processing correctness

slots.key: Expected response time for validation and updates
slots.value: Must handle bursts during business hours, end-of-month cycles, and campaign periods without delaying validation or routing updates

revisions.new_value: Must handle bursts during business hours, end-of-month cycles, and campaign periods without delaying validation or routing updates

slots.key: Accuracy expectations for portability state updates
slots.value: Must compare timestamps, transaction sequence, and source authority so older or out-of-order changes do not overwrite a newer confirmed state; updates outside tolerance or in the wrong sequence should be held for review or reprocessing, and the current state should be shown only after the update passes those checks and is confirmed as the latest valid one. If the incoming update has a clearly newer sequence or timestamp and matches the expected transaction context, accept it as the latest state; if timestamps are the same or sequence is out of order but the content still looks valid, hold it for operator review; if it conflicts with the active state in a way that suggests a duplicate, replay, or bad provider feed, reject it or send it back for reprocessing rather than applying it automatically.

slots.key: Exception handling for portability data discrepancies
slots.value: If there is a discrepancy, the operations team manages the exception and chases the originating provider rather than silently fixing the record without trace. Keep the issue open for provider action when the fix requires the originating provider to correct source data or confirm a disputed status. A temporary workaround or manual reconciliation is only appropriate if the issue is limited, reversible, can preserve an audit trail, and is clearly marked as provisional with a clear rollback; it should be time-limited and reviewed. The choice between leaving it open and using a workaround should be based on impact, urgency, and reversibility. If the mismatch affects live routing, a publish deadline, or a large set of records, a workaround can be justified when it can be safely isolated to one item; if it is just a reporting delay or low-priority discrepancy, leave it open for the originating provider to correct. A workaround without provider confirmation is acceptable only when the operational risk of waiting is higher than the risk of handling it temporarily ourselves.

slots.value: If a porting decision conflicts with a regulatory or industry rule, it must be escalated before routing is activated to the designated portability compliance contact or the industry authority that governs the numbering rules, depending on the operating model. The escalation path must be explicit and logged so routing does not proceed on an unapproved decision. The process should pause if the conflict could lead to an illegal port, wrong routing, or customer harm. It may continue provisionally only when the risk is low, the routing outcome is still reversible, and there is documented approval to proceed while escalation is pending.

slots.key: Unresolved exception handling at cutover
slots.value: If releasing an unresolved mapping issue at cutover would risk incorrect number routing, loss of service, or a breach of regulatory or provider agreement obligations, it must stay blocked and be escalated to a designated operations lead or duty manager for an explicit decision. It can only be released with a documented exception if the business owner accepts the risk, the impact is limited, and there is a clear rollback or correction path after cutover. The exception should only be triggered when the issue is low impact, tightly bounded to a specific record or small batch, and there is no material risk of wrong routing or service disruption if it proceeds. It also needs a clear compensating control, like a planned correction window, so it is not left open-ended. If the business owner is unavailable or declines to accept the risk, approval should fall to a delegated operations manager or duty executive with the same authority level; if no one at that level is reachable, the item should remain blocked. Frontline staff should not make that call on their own. The exception must record the reason, approver, and expiry or follow-up action so it does not become an unmanaged permanent state.

slots.key: Synchronization ownership for shared portability records
slots.value: The service management center owns the synchronization process and acts as the system of record for distributing and reconciling shared portability data. Participating providers remain responsible for submitting timely updates and corrections for the records they control, and the operations team handles discrepancies as exceptions by chasing the originating provider rather than silently fixing them. Updated portability data should go first to the networks directly affected by the change and needed for routing accuracy, especially the donor and recipient providers. Issues should be kept open for provider action when the fix requires the originating provider to correct source data or confirm a disputed status, since that is their accountability; a temporary workaround or manual reconciliation is only appropriate if the issue is limited, reversible, can preserve an audit trail without changing the underlying business truth, and is justified by impact, urgency, and reversibility. A workaround is acceptable without provider confirmation only when the operational risk of waiting is higher than the risk of temporarily handling it ourselves, the workaround can be isolated to one item with a clear rollback, it is clearly marked as provisional, time-limited, and reviewed, and it does not start to look like the wrong state has been accepted as normal. Low-priority discrepancies and reporting delays should be left open for the originating provider to correct.

slots.key: Normal publish cycle for clean portability records
slots.value: For clean records, distribution should happen as part of the normal publish cycle so everyone receives the same version at roughly the same time. If the record is complete, approved, and within the cutover window, it should go out in the next normal publish cycle without waiting for extra manual review. Delay it only if there is a pending validation run, a dependency on another record in the same batch, or the distribution window has already closed for that cycle; avoid holding clean records unnecessarily so participating networks stay aligned quickly.

slots.key: Controlled change release cadence and expedited change criteria
slots.value: Controlled changes should follow a regular scheduled release cadence, with expedited treatment reserved for urgent operational risk or active service-impacting conditions. An issue truly cannot wait when it is already causing failed port activations, incorrect routing, or a material backlog blocking customer moves, or when it affects multiple providers, has a compliance or service-level deadline within the current cycle, or is getting worse fast. If the issue is contained, has a safe workaround, and the next release is close enough that the business impact is manageable, it should wait for the next cycle. The threshold is whether delaying the fix creates a bigger operational or customer risk than releasing it early. For urgent bypass decisions, treat it as an immediate fix if the problem is stopping or corrupting live portability operations right now, including failed ports, wrong routing, or an uncontainable compliance exposure; defer it with a workaround when the impact is contained and the workaround preserves correct operation. Also prefer the workaround if rushing the change is likely to create a bigger outage than the original issue.

revisions.new_value: Controlled changes should follow a regular scheduled release cadence, with only well-tested, approved changes allowed into the shared portability process. An expedited path is acceptable only for urgent operational risk, and only with a documented impact assessment and explicit approval from the right operations authority. Business pressure alone is not sufficient to bypass normal control.

slots.key: Legacy record retention period after cutover
slots.value: Retain legacy records for a fixed policy window defined by the regulator, telecom rules, and internal records policy; once that window ends, the records can be disposed of unless there is a reason to hold them longer. Active disputes, audits, litigation, regulatory inquiries, fraud investigations, or legal holds pause disposal until formally cleared, and records should be retained longer if a case is still open or could reasonably become evidence.

slots.key: Partial-file hold and retention rules for sensitive records
slots.value: If only part of a file contains sensitive information, the hold should apply only to the relevant records or fields when they can be safely segregated without changing the meaning, context, or evidentiary value of the rest. The protected portion must remain unchanged until the hold is lifted, while non-sensitive parts follow normal retention and disposal rules. If the file cannot be reliably split, or if separation would break context, make the record incomplete, or create a risk of accidental disclosure, keep the whole file under hold. Sensitive material should remain access-controlled and redacted in ordinary views during the extended retention period. The practical rule is to preserve integrity and traceability while limiting access to only what needs protection.

slots.key: Confidentiality requirements for customer number data
Logging protection and sensitive data masking
slots.value: Transaction and audit records should be preserved for the required retention period and be tamper-evident because they may be used in disputes or regulator reviews; staff should see transaction identifiers, provider names, timestamps, current status, the decision trail, and any validation or exception notes tied to the case, while sensitive subscriber details such as full contact information, account content, or other unnecessary personal data should be masked or redacted unless higher clearance or a specific investigation justifies full visibility. Unmasking should only happen when the restricted data is genuinely necessary to resolve an active porting issue, such as a suspected fraud case, identity mismatch, dispute over ownership, or a regulatory review that cannot be completed with the limited view; it should not be opened for convenience or general curiosity. Before broader access is granted, approval is required from a designated supervisor, compliance lead, or security-controlled role, and the reason, the approver, who viewed the data, and how long elevated access was used must be logged in the case history.

slots.key: Correction history and amendment evidence retention
slots.value: Corrections to approved records should be authorized only by a limited set of privileged users, usually supervisors or designated operations leads rather than general staff. Each correction should include an attached reason and supporting evidence, such as a provider notice, audit reference, or ticket number. The original approved record should remain intact, and the correction should be saved as a new version or amendment entry rather than overwritten, to preserve a complete audit trail of what changed and who approved it.

revisions.new_value: If a correction happens later, the system must keep the full change history, the reason for the amendment, who approved it, and any source evidence or provider confirmation tied to that correction so the original decision and subsequent changes can be proven.

topics.topic_content: Operational maintenance and synchronization evolution

slots.key: Ongoing synchronization responsibilities
slots.value: Operationally, the service management center owns the synchronization process itself and acts as the system of record for distributing and reconciling shared portability data. Each participating provider remains responsible for sending timely updates and corrections for the records they control, and the operations team handles discrepancies as exceptions by chasing the originating provider rather than silently fixing them. Updated portability data should first go to the networks directly affected by the change and needed for routing accuracy, especially the donor and recipient providers. Records that are still under reconciliation or have an open exception should be held back from general distribution until the discrepancy is resolved or a formal exception is approved; for clean records, distribution should happen in the normal publish cycle so everyone receives the same version at roughly the same time. If one provider is out of sync, that specific record should be paused rather than pushing inconsistent data into the network.

slots.key: Audit trail completeness and retention expectations
slots.value: Migration must define core validation and retention rules before cutover so the process is safe and auditable. Every migrated record must be validated against the source, any exceptions must be logged, and the original import evidence must be retained for audit. The minimum rule should be clear enough to test what was accepted, what was rejected, and why; if a correction happens later, the system must keep the full change history, the reason for the amendment, who approved it, and any source evidence or provider confirmation tied to that correction, preserving the prior version rather than overwriting it. Corrections to approved records should be authorized only by a limited set of privileged users, usually supervisors or designated operations leads, not general staff, and must include an attached reason plus supporting evidence such as a provider notice, audit reference, or ticket number. Unresolved items should be blocked at cutover, escalated immediately, and accompanied by a formal hold and audit note; if only one record is unresolved, the delay decision should apply to that record rather than the whole migration. Transaction history and auditability are essential, supporting control and traceability, though they are behind live operational functions. Record request intake, validation result, status changes, conflicts raised, approvals or overrides, routing activation, retry or cancellation actions, and the final outcome, including who made each decision and when; if a workaround is used, capture the reason and whether it was temporary. Staff should see the transaction identifiers, the provider names involved, the timestamps, the current status, the decision trail, and any validation or exception notes tied to the case. Any active dispute, audit, litigation, regulatory inquiry, fraud investigation, or legal hold should pause disposal until it is formally cleared, and if a case is still open or could reasonably become evidence, it should be retained beyond the normal schedule. The hold should start when the matter is formally opened or when a written notice is received that identifies the case as subject to hold, whichever comes first. The opening notice or case ID should be stored against the affected records so it’s clear why disposal stopped. Exceptions to the hold audit trail should be narrow: system-generated changes may be shown without internal security details, and older actions that occurred before the hold was linked to a specific case may be visible only as a general timeline entry if they cannot reliably be tied to a person or matter. If anything is redacted, operations should still see that an action occurred, who or what role performed it if known, and the timestamp, even if the underlying sensitive note or reason text is hidden. Audit rules should document what is intentionally withheld versus what was never captured. If only part of the file needs to stay protected, the hold should apply just to the relevant records or fields, not necessarily the entire case file, as long as they can be segregated safely. The protected portion should be retained unchanged until the hold is lifted, while the non-sensitive parts should follow normal retention and disposal rules. If the file cannot be reliably split, the whole record set should remain under hold. Sensitive material should remain access-controlled and redacted in ordinary views during the extended retention period. For highly sensitive migration exports, logs should also capture what subset was exported, the exact purpose, whether it was encrypted or masked, and any transformation step like splitting, merging, or reformatting, along with who handled each step. If the export was later split into multiple files, the original export event must be tied to all derived files so the chain of custody is preserved. For normal sensitivity data, the log detail can be lighter, but for high-risk records this level of detail is mandatory.

The minimum rule should be clear enough to test what was accepted, what was rejected, and why; if a correction happens later, the system must keep the full change history, the reason for the amendment, who approved it, and any source evidence or provider confirmation tied to that correction, preserving the prior version rather than overwriting it. Corrections to approved records should be authorized only by a limited set of privileged users, usually supervisors or designated operations leads, not general staff, and must include an attached reason plus supporting evidence such as a provider notice, audit reference, or ticket number. Unresolved items should be blocked at cutover, escalated immediately, and accompanied by a formal hold and audit note; if only one record is unresolved, the delay decision should apply to that record rather than the whole migration. Transaction history and auditability are essential, supporting control and traceability, though they are behind live operational functions. Record request intake, validation result, status changes, conflicts raised, approvals or overrides, routing activation, retry or cancellation actions, and the final outcome, including who made each decision and when; if a workaround is used, capture the reason and whether it was temporary. Staff should see the transaction identifiers, the provider names involved, the timestamps, the current status, the decision trail, and any validation or exception notes tied to the case. Any active dispute, audit, litigation, regulatory inquiry, fraud investigation, or legal hold should pause disposal until it is formally cleared, and if a case is still open or could reasonably become evidence, it should be retained beyond the normal schedule.

slots.key: Cutover and legacy record retention
slots.value: The new system becomes the system of record at cutover, while old records are retained for reference and dispute handling for as long as business, regulatory, and audit requirements call for, with the retention period defined by policy rather than left open-ended. In practice, this should be a fixed policy window; once that window ends the records can be disposed of unless there is a reason to hold them longer. Access to legacy records should be tightly restricted to authorized operations, compliance, audit, and support staff, with normal users kept in the new system only. Staff should consult the old record for historical disputes, unresolved pre-cutover transactions, regulatory inquiries, and reconciliation issues between the old and new systems; for routine post-cutover ports with a clean history in the new system, they should rely on the new record alone.

slots.key: Compliance access controls and traceability

Exports should be limited to the minimum dataset needed. The log should capture the reason, requester, approver, timestamp, source record range, and destination or target system. If the task is sensitive, also log the file count or record count and whether any masking or encryption was applied.

slots.key: Regulatory compliance support and reporting
slots.value: The system should support whatever telecommunications portability regulations apply in the jurisdiction, including timely processing, accurate routing, and reporting support for compliance checks; exact legal retention periods and regulator-specific formats are pending confirmation from the compliance team. If a porting decision conflicts with a regulatory or industry rule, it must be escalated to the designated portability compliance contact or the industry authority governing numbering rules, depending on the operating model. The escalation path must be explicit and logged so routing does not proceed on an unapproved decision. Provisional continuation is only allowed when the port is operationally safe, with no likely misrouting or violation of a hard regulatory rule, typically for clerical issues, missing confirmation, or interpretation questions that can be corrected without changing the live routing outcome. It requires explicit approval from the designated compliance or operations authority, a documented reason, the risks accepted, the exact limits of the provisional action, and a time-bound record in transaction history for review or rollback.

slots.key: Operations console day-to-day tasks
slots.value: Review incoming provider requests, check validation results, resolve exceptions or conflicts, approve or correct records where authorized, monitor routing update and network distribution status, search transaction history, generate reports, and review audit trails when explanations are needed later. Staff should be able to use an exception queue so they do not have to hunt through routine work. Conflict resolution with clear status tracking is the next highest priority after receiving and validating provider requests, coordinating requests, activating routing changes, and distributing updated portability data. For exception or conflict handling, only designated operations staff with authority over number portability may resolve disputes, and in some cases an approved escalation owner may resolve them if providers cannot agree. If the conflict affects routing correctness or number ownership, work must pause until resolved; if it is only a documentation mismatch and live routing remains safe, a provisional decision may allow the process to continue. Regulatory or industry-rule issues require escalation before routing proceeds, especially where there is risk of violating porting rules or misrouting a live number. Immediate access to history is needed for provider disputes, suspected fraud or unauthorized ports, unresolved timeouts blocking the transaction, and manual override or reversal decisions. slots.key: Operations console usability factors
slots.value: The exception queue/review panel should highlight overdue or escalated items, with overdue items automatically escalating after a defined threshold. Items near cutover should be pushed to the top even if they arrived later. Items delayed on the team's side should be treated as more urgent than those simply waiting on an external provider, because the team can act on them immediately. Manual reordering by an authorized supervisor is allowed when there is a customer-impact reason, and the priority change must be logged so it is auditable. The external escalation path for regulatory or industry-specific conflicts still needs to be defined in the operating procedure.
